query: How does a refrigerator keep food cold?
answer:
A refrigerator doesn't make cold. It moves heat out of the box and lets it go into your kitchen, using a loop called the vapor-compression cycle [1][2].

A refrigerant flows through sealed tubing. When a liquid evaporates it soaks up heat, and the fridge depends on that. First, the compressor squeezes refrigerant gas, which makes it hot and high-pressure. That hot gas runs through the condenser coils on the back or bottom of the fridge. There it gives its heat to the room air and condenses into a liquid [2][3]. Next the liquid goes through a narrow capillary tube or expansion valve, which drops its pressure sharply. Lower pressure makes it much colder [1][3]. Finally the cold refrigerant enters the evaporator coils inside the fridge. It boils there, pulling heat out of the air and the food, and then returns as a gas to the compressor so the loop can start again [2][3].

A thermostat turns the compressor on and off to hold the set temperature. Insulated walls and door seals slow down how fast heat leaks back in. That's why the coils on the outside of a fridge feel warm.
